slides: Grief doesn't do stages. It comes in *waves.*
You can be fine for months. Then a song in the supermarket *flattens you.*
That's not going backwards. That's love *finding a way out.*
You don't have to fight the wave. Let it come. *Let it pass.*
Breathe out longer than you breathe in. Feet on the ground. *Ride it.*
The waves don't stop. They just come *further apart.*
And one day you catch yourself *smiling* at the thing that used to drown you.
Save this for the next wave. *Send it* to someone who's in one right now.
The last time you hold their hand, you *won't know* it's the last time.
I held my Supergran's hand. The next day I *said goodbye.*
Nobody tells you the ordinary days are the ones you'll *miss most.*
The cuddles. The laughs. Her saying *"the truth will always out."*
If you've still got someone you love, *don't wait.*
Make the visit. Ring them back. *Say the words* out loud.
Busy will still be there next week. *They might not.*
Send this to someone who needs to *make that call* today.
Nobody taught us what to do with grief. So we *worked through it.*
Longer hours. Another beer. *"I'm sweet, bro."*
But grief doesn't leave because you're busy. It just *waits for you.*
Tears aren't weakness. Our tūpuna knew that. *They're release.*
For years I never cried. When it finally came, it came *all at once.*
You don't have to fall apart in public. Just give it *somewhere to go.*
The car. The shower. A mate you trust. *Start there.*
Send this to the man who's been *"sweet"* a bit too long.
You're allowed to grieve the childhood you *never got.*
Nobody died. But something was *still lost.*
The safety. The softness. The adult who was *meant to show up.*
That grief is real, even if nobody ever *named it.*
Grieving it doesn't mean you hate your whānau. It means *you're being honest.*
The kid you were deserved more. *Say that out loud.*
Then give some of it back to them now. Rest. Play. *Protection.*
Send this to someone still grieving *a kid nobody looked after.*
Your body remembers the date *before you do.*
You wake up heavy and don't know why. Then you *check the calendar.*
Birthdays. Anniversaries. The first Christmas *with an empty chair.*
The firsts hit hardest. Nobody warns you about *the seconds* either.
You're not going backwards. Your body is *keeping the anniversary.*
Plan for those days. Tell someone. *Go easy* on yourself.
It's okay to laugh on those days too. *That's still love.*
Send this to someone with *a hard date* coming up.
You can grieve someone and still be *angry* at them.
Not every loss is a clean one. Some people hurt you *and* you loved them.
Relief and sadness can sit in the *same chest.*
You don't have to make them a saint to *miss them.*
You don't have to make them a monster to *be honest.*
Both things can be true. That's not confusion. *That's grief.*
Let it be as messy as the relationship *actually was.*
Send this to someone grieving *a complicated one.*
"Let me know if you need anything." They *won't.*
Grieving people can't make lists. They can barely *make dinner.*
So don't ask. *Just do* one thing.
Drop a feed at the door. Mow the lawns. Take the kids *for a few hours.*
Say their person's name. They're scared everyone will *forget.*
Keep showing up after the tangi. Month two is *the lonely bit.*
You don't need the right words. *Turning up* is the words.
Send this to the one who always asks *"what can I do?"*
